questions.stem: Where can a patient lose a large volume of blood with nothing visible externally?

options.text: Only into the abdomen
options.rationale: Several sites can conceal major volume.

options.text: The chest, abdomen, pelvis and the thighs
options.rationale: Correct, along with the ground under the patient.

options.text: Only into the chest
options.rationale: The abdomen, pelvis and thighs all conceal major loss too.

options.text: Nowhere — major bleeding is always visible
options.rationale: Major bleeding is frequently entirely concealed.

questions.stem: Which shock finding appears earliest?

options.text: Falling blood pressure
options.rationale: Pressure falls last, after compensation fails.

options.text: A rising pulse
options.rationale: Correct. It is the earliest and most useful sign.

options.text: Unconsciousness
options.rationale: A very late finding.

options.text: Visible bruising
options.rationale: Bruising takes hours to appear.

questions.stem: A patient after a fall has a pulse of 124, cold wet hands, a soft abdomen, no bruising, and a pressure of 128/76. How do you read this?

options.text: Reassuring — the abdomen is soft and the pressure is normal
options.rationale: Bruising takes hours and pressure falls last.

options.text: Compensated shock — the pulse and skin are the honest findings
options.rationale: Correct. Act on these rather than waiting for the pressure to fall.

options.text: No significant injury
options.rationale: The mechanism and the findings both say otherwise.

options.text: Anxiety after the fall
options.rationale: Cold clammy skin with a pulse of 124 is physiological.

questions.stem: How should the absence of bruising in the first hour be interpreted?

options.text: As evidence against internal bleeding
options.rationale: Bruising develops over hours; early absence means nothing.

options.text: As meaningless this early
options.rationale: Correct. The bruising that will be dramatic tomorrow is invisible now.

options.text: As proof the mechanism was minor
options.rationale: It proves nothing about the mechanism.

options.text: As a reason to delay transport
options.rationale: Never a reason to delay.

questions.stem: What treatment for internal bleeding is available to an EMT?

options.text: Direct pressure on the abdomen
options.rationale: Not an effective or appropriate intervention.

options.text: Oxygen as indicated, warmth, positioning, nothing by mouth, and rapid transport
options.rationale: Correct. The definitive treatment is a surgeon.

options.text: A tourniquet above the abdomen
options.rationale: Not possible or appropriate.

options.text: Oral fluids to replace the loss
options.rationale: Nothing by mouth; they may need theatre.

questions.stem: Why should you not spend scene time looking for a confirming sign?

options.text: Because signs are unreliable in every patient
options.rationale: Signs are useful; waiting for them is the problem.

options.text: Because the mechanism has already told you, and the treatment is elsewhere
options.rationale: Correct. Time spent confirming is time not spent travelling.

options.text: Because assessment is not an EMT function
options.rationale: Assessment very much is.

options.text: Because the hospital will repeat the assessment
options.rationale: That is true but is not the reason.

questions.stem: What is shock?

options.text: A blood pressure below a defined threshold
options.rationale: Hypotension is one late sign, not the definition.

options.text: Inadequate tissue perfusion
options.rationale: Correct. Defining it by pressure means recognising it late.

options.text: A psychological response to injury
options.rationale: That is a different use of the word.

options.text: Loss of more than half the blood volume
options.rationale: Shock occurs well before that.

questions.stem: What characterises compensated shock?

options.text: Low blood pressure with a slow pulse
options.rationale: That is neither phase.

options.text: Fast pulse, pale cool clammy skin, and a still-normal blood pressure
options.rationale: Correct. The normal number is the trap.

options.text: Normal pulse and normal skin
options.rationale: That is not shock.

options.text: Unresponsiveness with a very low pressure
options.rationale: That is decompensated shock.

questions.stem: An injured 9-year-old has a normal blood pressure, a fast pulse, slow capillary refill, and has gone quiet. How do you read this?

options.text: Stable, given the normal blood pressure
options.rationale: Children hold their pressure until they suddenly cannot.

options.text: Compensated shock in a child who may decompensate abruptly
options.rationale: Correct. The number is the least informative finding here.

options.text: Anxiety from the incident
options.rationale: Slow capillary refill is not anxiety.

options.text: Normal for a frightened child
options.rationale: Going quiet with these findings is not reassurance.

questions.stem: Why is keeping a bleeding trauma patient warm considered treatment?

options.text: Because comfort reduces anxiety
options.rationale: Comfort is a side benefit, not the reason.

options.text: Because cold blood clots poorly, and hypothermia and acidosis reinforce each other
options.rationale: Correct. Blankets are a clotting intervention here.

options.text: Because warmth raises blood pressure directly
options.rationale: Not the mechanism.

options.text: Because hospitals require normothermic patients
options.rationale: Not the rationale.

questions.stem: A shocked trauma patient complains of severe thirst. What do you do?

options.text: Give small sips of water

options.text: Withhold fluids — thirst itself is a sign of significant loss

questions.stem: How should a patient with a nosebleed be positioned?

options.text: Sitting up, head tilted back
options.rationale: This sends blood down the throat and causes vomiting.

options.text: Sitting up, leaning forward
options.rationale: Correct. Blood goes into a bowl rather than a stomach.

options.text: Lying flat
options.rationale: Lying flat also directs blood posteriorly.

options.text: Lying on the side with the head down
options.rationale: Not the recommended position for simple epistaxis.

questions.stem: Where exactly should the nose be pinched?

options.text: The bony bridge
options.rationale: Bone compresses nothing; the bleeding point is below it.

options.text: The soft cartilaginous part below the bone
options.rationale: Correct, squeezed firmly.

options.text: Both nostrils at the tip only
options.rationale: Too far forward to compress the bleeding point.

options.text: It should not be pinched at all
options.rationale: Pinching is the primary measure in simple epistaxis.

questions.stem: How long should compression be held?

options.text: One minute, then check
options.rationale: Checking resets the clock every time.

options.text: Thirty seconds at a time
options.rationale: Far too short to allow clot formation.

options.text: Until the patient says it has stopped
